meta.name: Castle Game - economy and colony data
meta.era: 12th century, the Holy Roman Empire's western borderlands (kept deliberately vague)

conventions.ids: snake_case, unique within each section. Every cross-reference uses ids.
conventions.name_vs_plain: 'name' is the period-accurate in-game name; 'plain' is the intuitive label used in tooltips and the serf menu.
conventions.quantities: All quantities, times and weights are placeholders for structure only. Balancing comes later, from the foundation up.
conventions.alternatives: In recipe inputs, 'a|b' means either a or b satisfies the slot.
conventions.special_jobs: 'self' = the occupant makes or fetches it themselves (needs are self-served).
conventions.status: 'proposed': true marks anything added in this pass that has not been agreed yet.
conventions.grades: Graded items (furniture, clothing, pottery) come in rough / improved / intricate. See mechanics.quality.

start.note: Arrival is game day 0. Autumn begins day 10, winter day 25, spring (the thaw) day 40.

0.2: Storage reworked. Stockpiles are now intermediate stores along a pathway. The Stockyard is the central store: Stock-House (goods kept inside), Open Yard (goods kept outside), Staging Area (deliveries in and out), Granary and Stable.

Stockman now runs the stockyard: reserves, scheduling deliveries with the count's carts and horses, and salting meat into barrels. Taming and breeding move to a new Herdsman (legacy Tamer), working from a Pinfold.
New serf jobs: Stock Hand (two posts: stockpile hand, one per stockpile; delivery hand), Stable Hand, Fisherman (lake, from a Fisherman's Hut). Hunters fish streams.
New noble: Quartermaster, head of the stockyards and stables late in the game. Steward keeps the wider economy.
Removed: Reeve (covered by the Stockman), brine springs, Salter and the Salt Works. Salt comes from the count's cart, then salt veins.
Needs are now provided by the stores and the cook. A colonist only fends for himself when they fail, which stalls his work; after the first winter it also costs mood, which carries into confidence.

Quality grades (rough / improved / intricate). Each class expects a grade. Serfs can make rough furnishings themselves in winter. Fine Clothing and Glazed Pottery became the intricate grade of Clothing and Pottery; Garb became Clothing.
Starting provisions from the count: a cart of salt, a second cart (planned), draught horses (planned).
Water sources split into streams and lakes. Fauna gained habitat and behaviour.
Hunters can take boar, wild goat and sheep, and cull wolves, foxes and bears. Beekeepers take wild swarms. Fish now come from the stream and lake entries.
0.3: Game start written out: the player and a messenger choose the site, the home stake goes down, the messenger leaves, then 13 serfs and a priest arrive with two carts and two horses. 15 people counting the player.
starting_provisions replaced by game_start: the opening sequence, who arrives, each person's kit, and the count's two carts.
New starting items: pickaxe, fishing rod, cooking pot, bucket, tinderbox. Each has a recipe for later.
Personal inventory: every colonist carries clothing and a cloak, and serfs and up keep the kit their job needs (jobs[].kit). Worn or missing kit becomes a demand from his house.
Priest added: arrives at the start, advises the player and keeps the chapel.

Stock hands all work for the stockyard. Stockpile hands go out to their assigned stockpile and move goods between it and the yard; delivery hands take the carts and horses to work sites, so builders don't walk to the stores for every item.
The first-winter grace ends at the spring thaw.
Weapons and armour are graded; grade sets durability and effectiveness.
Mining and quarrying need a pickaxe, fishing a rod, drawing water a bucket, cooking the pot.
0.4: Added the realm: premise, factions (Count, Duke, bandits, petty lords, agents), communication by messenger, justice, obligations to the Count, the attention ladder, and the loyalty choice.
Sheriff renamed Bailiff (a sheriff is a royal or comital officer, while a lord's own lands have a bailiff); he handles low justice for the player.
Added Messenger: the player's own riders to the Count and others. The Count's messenger at the start returns later as his envoy.
0.5: Setting: the Holy Roman Empire's western borderlands, not England. Count and Duke stand.
Clergy added as a fifth estate. The priest is the player's advisor and, secretly, the Count's man.
Loyalty: three paths (Count, Duke, his own), none forced.
How the lord falls depends on how he ruled. A just lord who still fails earns a new start with a loyal retinue (realm.legacy).
Espionage: information leaks from the far lands; the player can work out where from.
Story thread tracker (realm.threads): every running thread, what reveals it, and which systems it touches.
0.6: The player is not omniscient. He sees his people only through observation, asking around town, his counsel, and an end-of-day report built from what's known (mechanics.information).

Colony indices: weighted confidence (the only one the player gets a read on), and hidden prosperity, stability and legitimacy. Rebellion comes from the weighted consensus falling below a threshold, never from one malcontent (mechanics.colony_indices).
Ruling with an iron hand raises stability, deters crime disproportionately and pushes the rebellion point further out, while eating legitimacy.
The priest does not research; scholars come only from educated schoolmasters.
Kit is just what a colonist carries for his job; no carrying limits to manage.
The new start after a fall is deferred; the first run comes first. 'People's loyalty' is now legitimacy.
0.7: Skill progression: 17 skills on a 0-20 scale with four ranks (novice, apprentice, journeyman, master) tied to the quality grades. Every job states the skill levels it requires and the skill it trains; skill spills over into related skills, which is what carries a worker from one trade into the next (mechanics.skills, skills, jobs[].requires).
Promotion: the player assigns the opening work (hunter, gatherer, porter, woodcutter). Everything after comes from use, demand, a workplace and research; the player can cap how many move up a line.
Satisfaction bands: below 30% needs are failing (the biggest pull on confidence), 30-80% needs are being met, 80%+ needs are met and wants are being met.

Stability is the population's confidence averaged on a curve; it swings, and low stability means unrest up to riots. Legitimacy is the average of stability across the whole run: how much the people want to keep following the player.
Planned: personalities, which will drive dishonest or inaccurate reports and how people answer the player. The Duke can plant informants among men he sends or travellers the player takes in.
Letters are taught, not trained by a trade: at the school, or by the priest to a pupil or two early on.
0.8: Adopted: stability = consent + coercion; legitimacy averages consent only, and harsh acts count against it.
Decided: skills don't fade when unused. The 0-20 scale and spillover percentages stand for now.
Added mechanics.dynamics: the cause-and-effect graph from needs to legitimacy, drawn on the Dynamics tab.
Added mechanics.colony_indices.tuning: starting values for the curve constant k and the rates, for the Dynamics sandbox.
0.9: Legitimacy is now a long exponential moving average of consent (about 2.5 years of memory), less harsh acts, instead of a run-long average: slow to build and lose, but it still moves late in a run.
Added the mood trend: a one-season average of consent minus the long one (MACD-style). Hidden as a number, but it is what counsel and the people convey: warming to the lord, or souring.
Logged Elder Ray (bull and bear power against the trend) as a proposed trigger for local unrest from pockets of despair.
Dynamics sandbox runs up to six years, with an optional hard first year.
0.10: Patience adopted: a warming mood trend shifts the unrest bands down (people put up with more before rioting); a souring one shifts them up.
Pring's KST considered and set aside for now: in testing it wandered and flipped sign three times in a steady year, and needs 13 tuning values against the mood trend's two (colony_indices.ideas).
0.11: Proposed: asking around returns a Psychological Line of the people asked (the share who say things are better than last week) plus where each stands. Counsel keeps the slower mood trend.
0.12: Adopted: asking around returns the Psychological Line of those asked, averaged over a month (16 days; set to one 15-day season in 0.13).
Legitimacy starts at 80: the people come to follow; time tests it.
0.13: Calendar set: 15-day seasons, 60-day years. All tuning windows rescaled from the old 360-day assumption (a game year now passes six times faster).
Poll window set to one season (15 days), the nearest calendar unit to the month asked for.
Mood trend fast average: one season (15 days). Legitimacy memory: 2.5 years (150 days). Confidence rates and blame scaled so they behave the same per season as before.
0.14: The settlers arrive on the 5th day of summer: 11 days of summer, then autumn and winter; the spring thaw, which ends the first-winter grace, falls on day 41.
0.15: The settlers arrive on the 6th day of summer, not the 5th, so the document agrees with the game as built: 10 days of summer, then autumn and winter; the spring thaw falls on day 40.

changes_from_source: Colonist classes are now four: serf (base production), peasant (second-tier production), merchant (advanced production, runs establishments), noble (management). The old tier-2 merchant sub-list became merchant-class jobs with their own buildings.
Forester (wood gatherer) renamed Woodcutter. Forester is now a noble: keeper of the forest, herds and game, who sets the ecosystem protections.

Tree Farmer -> Woodward. Builder -> Wright ('Builder'). Craftsman -> split into Master Carpenter and Bowyer. Architect -> Master Mason. Stone Carver -> Carver. Engineer -> Ingeniator (the 12th-century term). Blacksmith -> Smith, with Smelter (Bloomer) added in front of it.

Tamer -> Stockman. Herdsman -> split into Herd Hand (serf) and Shepherd (peasant). Chef -> Master Cook. Brewer -> Brewster. Healer -> Herbalist, Doctor -> Leech, Surgeon -> Chirurgeon, Apothecary -> Spicer.

Student -> Clerk, Tutor -> Schoolmaster, Men at Arms -> Man-at-Arms (Serjeant), Treasurer -> Chamberlain, General -> Marshal, Quartermaster -> Steward, Researcher -> Scholar. Generic Merchant/Storekeeper -> Chapman.
Added jobs: Farm Hand, Herd Hand, Quarryman, Salter, Miller, Weaver, Chandler, Beekeeper, Smelter, Goldsmith, Moneyer, Draper, Reeve (proposed).

Added buildings: Smithy, Bloomery, Storehouse, Granary, Stockyard, Windmill, Watermill, Fulling Mill, Well, Mine Head, Salt Works, Lime Kiln, Masons' Lodge, Sheepfold, Byre, Sty, Hen House, Apiary, Mint, Market, School, Scriptorium. Every dwelling and workshop has upgrade tiers.
Added zones: forest, hunting ground, orchard, farm, pasture, quarry, clay pit, mine, salt works, craft quarter, merchant street, storage yard, manor.
Fixed: duplicate MEAT and SALT; cow domestication gave wool (now milk); AXE 'requires woodsman' (now wood + iron).

Added resources: flour (mills), lime (mortar), roof tile, leather (soft, before hard leather), parchment (books are parchment in the 12th c, not fibre), linen and woollen cloth (replacing light and heavy cloth), tallow, candle, pottage, arrows, feathers, seeds, livestock.
Bread no longer needs egg (plain bread is flour, water and salt; eggs go into pastry). Desserts -> Pastry. FOOD split into Pottage (basic) and Quality Meal.

Accuracy flags, kept but gated or renamed: Long Bow -> War Bow (the classic English longbow is 13th-14th c); Poleaxe -> Bill (poleaxe is 15th c); Hammer -> Mace; Iron Armor -> Mail Hauberk (12th c armour is mail, not plate); Cloth Armor -> Gambeson; Brick is gated behind research (rare in 12th-c England). Crossbow added (12th c, gated).
Flax added as flora (the source had fibre with no plant producing it); Wild Boar and Pig added (the commonest medieval meat animal).
open_questions: How fast should confidence chase satisfaction, falling and rising? The sandbox defaults are guesses.
Which harsh acts count, and how much each: a hanging, a flogging, seizing stores, forced labour?
k is to be found by trial and error against target cases (e.g. 2 of 15 in despair: grumbling, not riots). Default 4.
Elder Ray for local unrest: worth adding, given the k curve already weights the unhappy?

realm.premise: The player is a minor noble, promoted by the Count to oversee and develop his far lands. As their lord he arrives with a retinue of serfs to do his bidding and basic provisions for the first winters. After a few years the Count begins taxing the lands' production.
realm.hidden_truth: The Count is developing the far lands to raise his own station. The new Duke dislikes him and a secret rivalry has formed; the Count wants the lands' success to strengthen his legitimacy, and the player is the only promising minor noble at his court he can trust with the task. The player doesn't know any of this at the start.

player.title: Lord of the far lands
player.role: Delegate and manage the colony as it grows: daily life, the roads and his people's security, winters, taxes, fighting forces, and a stronghold, while being drawn into the rivalry.

factions.name: The Count
factions.wants: Accounts, renders (taxes on production after a few years), military service when summoned; secretly, a prosperous march that raises his standing against the Duke.
factions.methods: Messengers with demands that sharpen as the Duke's pressure on him grows; threats of replacement or forfeiture. His priest in the far lands reports back to him.
factions.hidden_motive: Legitimacy in his rivalry with the Duke.

factions.name: The Duke
factions.wants: To pry the far lands away from the Count.
factions.methods: Practical aid: seed after a bad harvest, a few skilled men, protection against a common threat; gifts and flattering letters.

factions.name: Bandits and outlaws
factions.methods: Probe for weakness on the roads and at the edges first.

factions.name: Neighbouring petty lords and freebooters
factions.wants: An easy target or a useful buffer.

factions.name: Agents and informants
factions.wants: To report on the colony's output and the player's leanings.
factions.methods: Travellers, merchants, settlers, men at court.

factions.name: The Church
factions.wants: Tithes, a chapel worthy of the lands, a say in their morals.
factions.methods: Through the priest; later through requests for more clergy.

attention_ladder.rule: Prosperity draws eyes in roughly this order. Triggers include cleared land, surplus grain, livestock, a stronger hall, and rumours of a mine or good timber. Each new party arrives with incomplete information and its own agenda.

rungs.notes: Once the colony's output is noticed at court, both the Count's and the Duke's.

communication.messengers: Messengers on foot or horseback are the only link. In hard country a round trip takes weeks.
communication.failure: Letters can be lost, delayed, intercepted, or deliberately held back by either side.
communication.consequence: The Count receives filtered, out-of-date reports. The player learns of new pressures only when a messenger arrives, or when armed men appear on the road, and must often decide before he can consult anyone.
communication.rumour: Rumours travel faster than facts. A delayed report or an intercepted gift can read as treason to one side and prudence to the other.
communication.ui_note: Every letter and report carries the date it was written, so the player sees how stale his news is.

justice.low: The player (or his bailiff) settles disputes among the serfs by customary right: theft, land quarrels, assaults, inheritance fights as the colony grows.
justice.high: High justice (hanging, mutilation) is the Count's in theory. Distance and urgency mean a remote lord often does it anyway and seeks approval later, or hopes no one important complains.
justice.risk: Taking high justice yourself is practical but can be used against you if it reaches the Count, or the Duke.

authority.day_to_day: Unchecked: for practical purposes the player is the highest authority on the ground.
authority.limits: Not immune forever. The Count expects periodic accounts, military service when summoned, and renders. Total silence or open defiance will eventually force him to act; the cost of projecting power into harsh terrain buys time and leverage.

loyalty.choice: The player owes nothing he must honour. He can keep faith with the Count, go over to the Duke, or take his own path to secure his own position.

paths.name: Keep faith with the Count
paths.pressure: Demands grow as the Duke presses the Count; threats of replacement or forfeiture.

paths.name: Go over to the Duke
paths.pressure: The easy road: gifts and provisions now, the Count's enmity and the Duke's terms later.

paths.name: His own path
paths.pressure: Play both, stall behind slow messengers, or hold the far lands for himself once they can defend themselves; both great lords become a threat.

loyalty.pressure: The Duke sways with gifts and provisions. The Count, pressed harder by the Duke, demands more and more.

arc.focus: Feed, house and clothe the retinue; first bandits.
Surplus, trades, the first appointments; renders begin; petty lords take notice.
Agents of both lords; the Duke's first gifts; the Count's demands sharpen.
Loyalty forced into the open; stronghold and fighting forces decide the outcome.

realm.setting: The Holy Roman Empire's western borderlands, 12th century. Details kept vague.

legacy.rule: Every path can end in ruin. How the player ruled decides what kind.
legacy.people_loyalty: Legitimacy (mechanics.colony_indices) builds slowly from how the lord treats his people. It is hidden from the player.

outcomes.fall: Tyrannical and uncaring: when he falls, he falls alone. No one stands with him.
His people stand by him through failure. A lord who did right and still fails earns the right to start again: a new map, a new home, and his loyal retinue following him.

legacy.notes: Deferred: the first run comes first. The fall-alone versus stand-by-him outcomes stay as the intent.

espionage.premise: Information flows out of the far lands to the Count and, later, to the Duke. The Count's man is the priest.
leak_sources: messengers (read or bribed on the road)
espionage.what_leaks: Output, stores, men under arms, the player's letters and leanings, how he dispenses justice.
player_counterplay: Notice what the Count knows that he shouldn't
Feed false information and see where it surfaces
espionage.rule: Each lord knows the far lands only through what reaches him: reports, leaks and rumour, never the true stock numbers. Hidden output works until it's found out.

threads.name: The Count-Duke rivalry
revealed_through: the changing tone of the Count's letters

threads.name: Why the Count needs the far lands
The priest is the Count's man
revealed_through: what the Count knows that he shouldn't

threads.name: Taxes and hidden output
revealed_through: the Count's demands begin after a few years

threads.name: Order versus legitimacy
revealed_through: who stands by him in a crisis

realm.threads_note: A thread tracker for keeping the story consistent while it's written: each thread, how the player learns of it, and which systems it depends on.

sequence.what: The player, a minor noble newly made lord of the Count's far lands, rides the map with the Count's messenger looking for a place to settle.
The player places the home stake. The messenger rides back to fetch the retinue; he returns later as the Count's envoy.
On the 6th day of summer the settlers arrive: 13 serfs and the priest, with two carts and two horses. Fifteen people in all, counting the player. They have 40 days to the thaw.
The player marks stockpiles, the habitation zone and pathways, and assigns the opening jobs.

colonists.notes: Unassigned on arrival; the player assigns opening jobs by aptitude.

personal_kit.notes: Winter clothes and a cloak on every back. Job tools are handed out from the carts when jobs are assigned.

carts.name: Stores cart
carts.notes: Salt for packing meat until a salt vein is mined, seed grain, and food to bridge the first days.

carts.name: Kit cart
carts.notes: Camp pot, fire, and the opening jobs' tools. 'Tools' covers the builders' generic kit.

game_start.later: Once travelling merchants and politics are in, anything else can be bought, bartered, given as a gift, or requested from the count.

classes.name: Serf
classes.role: Base production. Gathers raw resources and makes low-quality goods. Creates the colony's wealth.
classes.notes: Unpaid; provided for from the stores like everyone else. Last in the queue for wants, but their wants are few and rough-grade, and they can make rough furnishings themselves in winter. As colony wealth rises their expectations rise, or they turn rebellious.

classes.name: Peasant
classes.role: Second-tier production. Tradesmen who turn raw resources into goods, and wage-paid service roles (guards, clerks).
classes.assigned_by: skill progression for trades; player appointment for wage roles
classes.notes: A peasant tradesman's workshop is also his house, so his household places demand on the stockpile for his inputs.

classes.name: Merchant
classes.role: Advanced production. Masters who run establishments in player-designated merchant zones, oversee the movement of goods, and create labour demand for peasants and serfs.
classes.assigned_by: player appointment (requires coin and the supply window showing the village can support the role)
classes.notes: Appointing too early or below the skill threshold pulls workers off base production. Pulling a merchant back to basic work makes him unhappy and his building falls into disrepair.

classes.name: Noble
classes.role: Management. Officials who take whole areas off the player's hands (treasury, law, forest, army, supply, research).
classes.notes: Wages come from the coffers and return through purchases and taxes.

classes.name: Clergy
classes.role: A separate estate outside the ladder of production. The priest keeps the chapel, advises the lord, and answers to the Church and to whoever placed him.
classes.assigned_by: arrives with the colony; later clergy by request to the Church or the Count
classes.notes: Stands apart from serf, peasant, merchant and noble. Can move between them as confessor and counsellor, which is also what makes him a good informant.

needs.name: Nourishment
needs.notes: Food value by item; cooked food better than raw.

needs.name: Rest
needs.notes: Sleeping on the ground meets the need poorly.

needs.name: Shelter
needs.notes: Habitation builds itself in the habitation zone to meet this.

wants.rule: Wants are pursued only once needs are met. Each class has a set of wanted items and an expected grade (classes[].want_grade). An item at the expected grade or above meets the want fully; a lower grade meets it partly.
wants.placed_by: The dwelling, not the person. The house places the demand on the supply chain for its occupants' wants.
wants.queue: Serfs come last, but their wants are few and rough-grade, so a working colony meets them easily. More complex wants need more complex jobs and buildings.

states.formula_sketch: confidence moves toward satisfaction over time, falling fastest when satisfaction is under 30%, minus blame (fending for himself after the first winter) and shocks
states.effects: Each colonist's confidence feeds stability. A serf whose needs are met keeps solid confidence even when his wants aren't.

states.formula_sketch: mood (satisfaction) = needs met first, then wants; see mechanics.satisfaction for the bands
states.effects: Satisfaction scales work speed and skill gain, and pulls on confidence, hardest below 30%.
General modifier on work speed, mood and confidence. Restored by care.

supply_chain.summary: Demand is placed by buildings, filled from the stockyard by the stockman's deliveries, and held as deficits against reserves that pass up the chain to the job that makes the item. Goods flow back down through stockpiles to the stockyard.

stages.action: An unmet need or want becomes a demand from the dwelling (a serf wants a trestle table, so his hovel requests one).
If the stock-house or open yard holds it above reserve, the stockman schedules a delivery from the staging area. A delivery hand takes it, by cart and horse when the load or distance warrants.
If not, the deficit places a demand on the job whose recipe makes the item (trestle table -> carpenter).
The producer's workshop-house requests the recipe inputs; the stockman stages and delivers them (wood to the carpenter).
If that takes stock under its reserve, the deficit places demand on the raw producer (wood -> woodcutter).
The gatherer drops his goods at the nearest stockpile. The stockpile hand the yard has assigned there moves them on to the stockyard, where they re-enter the stocks.
Building materials go to the work site by cart, so builders keep building instead of walking to the stores for every item.

priority: needs of all classes (injured and starving first)
supply_chain.reserves: The player sets reserve levels early; the stockman keeps them, and late game the quartermaster.

chain: serf_dwelling (want: trestle_table) -> stockman: none in the stock-house
carpenter_workshop requests wood x3 -> stockman stages it, delivery hand delivers
open yard wood under reserve -> woodcutter (recipe fell_tree)
woodcutter drops logs at the forest stockpile -> stockpile hand carts them to the open yard
carpenter makes the table -> delivery hand takes it to the hovel -> want met, mood up
or, in winter, the serf makes a rough table himself (make_rough_trestle_table)

progression.skill_gain: By use, fastest in the job done, slower in related jobs by weighted spillover.
progression.promotion: A job opens when demand exists, the workplace exists (or can be built) and research allows it. The most capable worker moves in.
progression.reversion: If an input runs short, dependent trades revert to their upstream job (see each job's reverts_to).
progression.pressure_from_below: Skilled workers become unhappy if the town doesn't progress to meet their new demands; unmet needs make them leave.

needs_rule.provided: Everyone, serfs included, meets needs from the colony's system first: food from the stock-house and the cook, rations, water, beds and fires in their homes.
needs_rule.fend_for_self: If the system can't provide a need, the colonist leaves his job to fend for himself (forage, hunt, find shelter). Production stalls and time is wasted.
needs_rule.blame: Grace through the first winter, which ends at the spring thaw (day 40 from arrival). After it, every time someone has to fend for himself his mood drops, and that drop carries into confidence: he blames the player.
needs_rule.overextension: Opening jobs, appointments and buildings faster than manpower and stores can carry means people go unprovided and suffer.

quality.rule: Graded items carry a grade. A job's skill sets the highest grade it can make (jobs[].max_grade). A recipe may fix the grade (recipes[].grade). For weapons and armour, grade sets durability and effectiveness.

grades.name: Rough
grades.made_by: the occupant himself (winter work) or any apprentice tradesman

inventory.rule: Every colonist keeps his own kit: clothing and a cloak, plus the tools his job needs (jobs[].kit). Kit is simply what he carries for his job; job placement keeps it sensible, so there are no carrying limits to manage.
inventory.wear: Kit wears with use. A worn or missing item becomes a demand from his house, filled by the stockman like any other.
inventory.job_change: On changing job he returns kit he no longer needs to the stockyard and asks for the new job's kit.

information.rule: The player is not omniscient and gets no menu that spoon-feeds him everything. He knows his people and stores only through what reaches him.

sources.what: What the player sees for himself as he moves about.

Walking the town and asking people how things are. Each says where he stands (hungry, getting by, content) and whether things are better than last week. The share who say better, averaged over the last season (15 days) of answers, is the Psychological Line the player hears.

Reports, opinions and advice from his counsel: the priest at first, later his officials. Each counsellor has his own view, and the priest his own master. Conveys the slower mood trend: warming or souring.
End of day: stocks, production and changes, compiled from the information available, not from the true numbers.

proposed: A report is only as good as its reporter: a less skilled stockman or steward gives rougher figures; a dishonest one gives slanted ones.
Figures from distant stockpiles arrive late.

colony_indices.rule: Colony-wide measures built from every colonist. The player gets only a general consensus, through his information sources.

indices.visible: as a general read, via counsel, reports and asking around
indices.built_from: The player's impression of how his people are: an approximation of consent, as good as his sources.
Consent (the population's confidence averaged on a curve, weighting the most dissatisfied) plus coercion (harshness, hangings, guards). Swings with events.
indices.sketch: weight_i = 1 + k * (1 - confidence_i / 100)^2; consent = sum(weight_i * confidence_i) / sum(weight_i); stability = consent + coercion
indices.drives: How unruly the population can become: grumbling, crime, unrest, riots, rebellion.

indices.built_from: A long exponential moving average of consent (about 2.5 years, 150 days, of memory), with each day under harsh rule counting for less. Starts high (80): the people come to follow; time tests it.
indices.drives: How much the people want to keep following the player in the long run (realm.legacy).

indices.visible: as a sense, never a number: counsel and people say the mood is warming or souring
indices.built_from: A fast average of consent (one season, 15 days) minus the slow one (the legitimacy memory), like the MACD study.
indices.drives: What counsel reports and what people say when asked, and patience: how much they'll bear before unrest.
The attention ladder: who comes looking.

rebellion.trigger: Stability falling through the bands. It never rests on one dissatisfied man.
rebellion.threshold_moved_by: Coercion: harsh rule holds order at lower confidence.

iron_hand.why_it_pulls: Most of the cost is hidden: the player sees order and output, not the legitimacy draining away.

consent_and_coercion.rule: stability = consent + coercion. Consent is the curve-weighted confidence of the population; coercion comes from harshness, hangings and guards. Legitimacy is a long moving average of consent only, and harsh acts count against it directly.
consent_and_coercion.why: If legitimacy is simply the run-long average of stability, then force that props up stability also props up legitimacy, and the iron hand costs nothing.

tuning.note: Starting guesses for trial and error. Days are game days: 15 per season, 60 per year.
tuning.k_rule_of_thumb: One person at zero confidence weighs as much as (1 + k) content people. Pick that number and subtract one.

ideas.name: Elder Ray (local unrest)
ideas.what: Bull power = how far the best-off sit above the consent trend; bear power = how far the worst-off sit below it.
ideas.use: Deep bear power in one group or district (a starving row of hovels while the colony looks fine) triggers local trouble: a riot in one quarter, a work refusal, a theft spree.
ideas.caution: The k curve already weights the unhappy; using both on the same number would count them twice.

ideas.name: Pring's KST (Know Sure Thing)
ideas.what: Weighted sum of four smoothed rates of change over short to long lookbacks, with a signal line.
ideas.finding: On a scripted six-year run it wandered in a steady year (three sign flips, sitting at -2.4 with nothing happening), its signal-line cross took 518 days to flag a year of tyranny, and it needs 13 tuning values. The two-average mood trend was steady when nothing changed, caught tyranny in 19 days, and needs two.
ideas.revisit_if: The mood trend proves too twitchy in play and a multi-timescale blend is wanted.

ideas.name: Psychological Line (asking around)
ideas.what: Share of people who say things are better than last week, among those the player asks.
ideas.use: The reading the player gets from asking around, averaged over a season (15 days) of answers.
ideas.finding: Across people, it read 0% within a week of tyranny and 93-100% in recovery, while the mood trend still pointed the wrong way four weeks in. Over time (the classic form) it barely registered tyranny, so it isn't used that way.

patience.rule: A warming mood trend gives people patience: the stability levels at which grumbling turns to unrest and riots shift down. A souring trend shifts them up.
patience.sketch: band_shift = clamp(-mood_trend * patience_per_trend_point, -patience_max, +patience_max); judge the stability bands at (stability - band_shift)

satisfaction.rule: Each colonist's satisfaction (0-100%) says how well his needs, then his wants, are being met. It is what the player hears about as 'how people are doing'.

bands.meaning: Needs are being met, to a varying degree.
bands.effect_on_confidence: Mild pull below the middle of the band, neutral above.

bands.meaning: Needs are met and wants are being met as well.

drives: Honest, slanted or wrong reports from counsel and officials
Whether people tell the player the truth, avoid him, or say what he wants to hear
Who can be bought or planted as an informant

ranks.meaning: Can do the work slowly and roughly.
Reliable at the trade's basic work.
Master of the trade; may need tools or research to reach.

skills.proficiency: Each colonist starts with base levels in every skill (0-5), seeded by background.
skills.aptitude: Each colonist has a growth multiplier per skill (about 0.5-1.5). The serf menu shows both.
skills.gain: By use: the job's main skill grows fastest, and a weighted share spills into related skills (skills[].spillover). Gain slows at higher levels.
skills.caps: Some skills can't pass a level until research or tools allow (skills[].master_needs).

taught.letters: No trade builds letters. They're taught: at the school by the schoolmaster, or by the priest to a pupil or two before there is a school. Anyone the player sends to lessons loses that time from work.

promotion: A role opens when demand exists, its workplace exists or can be built, and research allows it.
Candidates are workers who meet the job's requirements (jobs[].requires), preferring those already in a job it rises from (jobs[].from).
The best candidate by skill and aptitude moves up; his old job is refilled from below.
If his inputs run short he reverts to the upstream job (jobs[].reverts_to).
player_controls: Assigns each serf's first work: hunter, gatherer, porter or woodcutter, by aptitude. This is the primary delegation.
Can cap how many move up a line, so raw producers always remain.
Appoints wage roles (guards, clerks, merchants, nobles); skill still has to meet the requirement.
skills.decay: None: skills don't fade when unused.

dynamics.note: Cause and effect between needs, the people's states and the colony's indices. 'seen' marks what reaches the player; everything else is behind the scenes.

nodes.label: Needs met
nodes.detail: Food, drink, rest, shelter, warmth, clothing, care: from the stores, the cook and the home.

nodes.label: Wants met
nodes.detail: Class wants at the class's grade, once needs are met. Serfs come last.

nodes.label: Fending for himself
nodes.detail: When the stores fail. Stalls work; after the spring thaw it also turns into blame.

nodes.label: Shocks
nodes.detail: Raids, deaths, unpaid wages, broken promises.

nodes.label: Iron hand
nodes.detail: The player's harshness: hangings, floggings, seizures, guards at every corner.

nodes.label: Satisfaction
nodes.detail: Per colonist, 0-100%: under 30 failing, 30-80 provided, 80+ content.

nodes.label: Confidence
nodes.detail: Per colonist. Chases satisfaction, falling fastest below 30%.

nodes.label: Consent
nodes.detail: The population's confidence, curve-weighted so the most unhappy count more (k).

nodes.label: Mood trend
nodes.detail: Fast minus slow average of consent: warming or souring. Felt through counsel and people, never shown as a number.

nodes.label: Stability
nodes.detail: consent + coercion. Swings. How unruly the people can become.

nodes.label: Legitimacy
nodes.detail: Long moving average of consent (about 2.5 years), less harsh acts. Whether they want to keep following him.

nodes.label: Work speed, skill gain
nodes.detail: Content workers work faster and learn faster.

nodes.label: Stand by him, or he falls alone
nodes.detail: Who stays through famine, raids and failure.

nodes.label: Crime, riots, rebellion
nodes.detail: Stability bands: orderly, grumbling, unrest, rebellion.

nodes.label: What the lord hears
nodes.detail: A general consensus via counsel, asking around and the daily report. Later bent by personalities and informants.

skills.name: Building
skills.covers: Raising timber, wattle and thatch buildings.

skills.name: Gathering
skills.covers: Foraging plants, herbs, honey and wax.

skills.name: Mining
skills.covers: Digging ore, coal and salt; smelting.

construction_tiers.name: Wood and Thatch
construction_tiers.features: Post-and-plank walls, plank or earth floor, thatched roof, open central hearth or campfire outside.

construction_tiers.name: Cruck Frame, Wattle and Daub
construction_tiers.features: Cruck-framed, daubed walls, thatch, central hearth, shuttered window.

construction_tiers.name: Timber Frame on Stone Footing
construction_tiers.features: Stone sill, timber frame, plank floor, upper loft, tiled or shingled roof, stone hearth.

construction_tiers.name: Stone
construction_tiers.features: Stone walls, vaulted undercroft, fireplace with chimney, glazed or shuttered windows.

zones.name: Home Stake
zones.purpose: Placed by the player at the start; the centre of the village. Radiates a priority gradient: nearer buildings improve first.

zones.name: Pathway / Road
zones.purpose: All buildings must attach to a pathway. Upgrades: footpath -> cart track -> metalled road (stone).

zones.name: Habitation
zones.purpose: Self-building housing along pathways for serfs and peasants (crofts).
zones.rules: Minimum footprint per resident (~5 x 5 m living space for a serf). Set back 0.25-1 m from the path.

zones.name: Merchant Street
zones.purpose: Burgage plots: narrow frontages on a main road, shop at the front, house behind/above. Merchants' establishments go here.

zones.name: Craft Quarter
zones.purpose: Peasant workshop-houses. Noxious trades (tannery, shambles, bloomery, lime kiln) are placed at the edge, downwind or downstream.

zones.name: Stockpile
zones.purpose: Intermediate store along a pathway, near where goods are gathered. Gatherers drop goods here; a stock hand from the yard moves them on.
zones.rules: Must touch a pathway. The stockyard assigns one stock hand to each stockpile; he works for the yard, not the pile.

zones.name: Stockyard
zones.purpose: The colony's central store, run by the stockman: the stock-house for goods kept inside, the open yard for goods kept outside, the staging area for deliveries in and out, the granary, and the stable for the cart horses.

zones.name: Forest
zones.purpose: Woodland worked by woodcutters, replanted and coppiced by the woodward, protected under the forester.

zones.name: Hunting Ground
zones.purpose: Where hunters may take game. The forester sets culling limits and protected species.

zones.name: Orchard
zones.purpose: Fruit trees planted by the woodward, picked by gatherers. Protected from felling.

zones.name: Farm (Open Field)
zones.purpose: Arable land in strips under a three-field rotation: winter grain, spring crop (vegetables, flax), fallow (grazed and manured). Needs water: next to a source, a player-dug channel, or a well.
zones.rules: Fields beyond irrigation reach yield less in dry seasons. Fallow strips count as pasture.

zones.name: Pasture
zones.purpose: Fenced grazing (wattle hurdles) for sheep, cattle, goats, pigs and horses, worked by herd hands and the shepherd.
zones.rules: Capacity = grass regrowth per area. Overgrazing lowers it.

zones.name: Quarry
zones.purpose: Open stepped pit where rock is exposed. Quarrymen cut rock; the mason's yard should sit nearby.

zones.name: Clay Pit
zones.purpose: Dug near water. Porters dig clay for daub, pottery and tiles.

zones.name: Mine
zones.purpose: Placed on the visible start of a vein (iron, coal, salt). Starts as bell pits, deepens to shored shafts. Gold and silver lie along the common veins, deeper.

depth_stages.notes: Shallow pit widened at the bottom; abandoned when unsafe.
Timber shoring; wet strata need more.
Needed for gold and silver at depth.

zones.name: Waterside
zones.purpose: Stream and lake banks: watermills and the fulling mill on streams, the fisherman's hut on a lake shore.

zones.name: Guard Post
zones.purpose: Guardhouses at roads and gates; later walls.

zones.name: Manor
zones.purpose: The player's seat and the nobles' halls. The only area where the player has direct building control.

buildings.name: Croft
buildings.notes: Toft (house plot) and croft (garden). For peasants whose work isn't in a workshop (wright, herders, guards).

buildings.name: Manor (Player's Seat)
buildings.notes: Player has direct control over layout here.

buildings.name: Stock-House
buildings.notes: Goods that must be kept indoors. Meat is salted and packed into barrels here.

buildings.name: Open Yard
buildings.notes: Goods that can stay outside: wood, rock, ore, coal, clay, straw.

buildings.name: Staging Area
buildings.notes: Deliveries to and from the stocks are assembled and loaded here.

buildings.name: Granary
buildings.notes: Raised floor keeps vermin and damp out.

buildings.name: Well
buildings.notes: Placed using the aquifer heat map.

buildings.name: Cookhouse
buildings.notes: Communal kitchen before bakers and inns exist.

buildings.name: Mason's Yard
buildings.notes: Dresses rock into stone blocks. Best placed near the quarry.

buildings.name: Masons' Lodge
buildings.notes: Drawing floor for advanced structures; produces castle blocks.

buildings.name: Farmstead
buildings.notes: Base for the farm hands; holds seed grain and tools.

buildings.name: Windmill
buildings.notes: Post mills appear in England in the 1180s.

buildings.name: Watermill
buildings.placement: On a river or stream; mill race dug by the player.
buildings.notes: Grinds faster than the windmill and runs in calm weather.

buildings.name: Fisherman's Hut
buildings.placement: Lake shore, placed by the player.

buildings.name: Pinfold
buildings.notes: Pound where wild animals are tamed and stock is bred before going out to pasture.

buildings.name: Stable
buildings.notes: Houses the count's draught horses first, later riding horses and knights' mounts.

buildings.name: Tannery
buildings.placement: Downstream, at the edge of the village.

buildings.name: Fulling Mill
buildings.effect: Raises woollen cloth output and quality for every weaver.

buildings.name: Mine Head
buildings.notes: Tier follows the mine's depth stage.

buildings.name: Bloomery
buildings.placement: Near the mine or at the craft quarter edge.

buildings.name: Market
buildings.notes: Replaces the General Store. Where travelling merchants trade and surplus is sold.

buildings.name: Chapel
buildings.effect: Mood bonus to residents within reach.
buildings.notes: The priest lives beside his chapel.

jobs.name: Woodcutter
jobs.description: Fells trees for wood and saplings and carries logs to the stockpile.

jobs.name: Hunter
jobs.description: Stalks game with a self bow, brings home meat, hides and feathers; fishes streams.

jobs.name: Fisherman
jobs.description: Fishes a lake from the fisherman's hut with nets and lines.

jobs.name: Gatherer
jobs.description: Forages berries, mushrooms, herbs, wild vegetables, wild grain, flax and fruit.

jobs.name: Porter
jobs.description: Draws water and digs clay. Opening job; hauling passes to the stock hands once there is a stockyard.

jobs.name: Stock Hand

posts.name: Stockpile Hand
posts.duty: Sent by the yard to an assigned stockpile; moves goods between it and the stockyard.

posts.name: Delivery Hand
posts.duty: Takes the carts and horses to work sites, workshops and homes when a load or distance calls for it.

jobs.description: Works for the stockyard. Moves goods between the stockpiles and the yard, and delivers to homes, workshops and work sites.

jobs.name: Stable Hand
jobs.description: Tends the stable; feeds, waters and harnesses the cart horses.

jobs.name: Quarryman
jobs.description: Cuts rock from the quarry face.

jobs.name: Miner
jobs.description: Digs iron ore, coal and rock salt; gold and silver once shafts are deep enough.

jobs.name: Farm Hand
jobs.description: Ploughs, sows, weeds, reaps and threshes the open-field strips.

jobs.name: Herd
jobs.description: Drives stock to pasture, milks, gathers eggs, mucks out byre and sty.

jobs.name: Woodward
jobs.description: Plants saplings, coppices woodland, tends the orchard and makes wattle hurdles.

jobs.name: Wright
jobs.description: Builds and repairs timber, wattle and thatch buildings (tiers 1-3).

jobs.name: Carpenter
jobs.description: Makes furniture, barrels, tool handles and mine shoring.

jobs.name: Stockman
jobs.description: Runs the stockyard and stock-house: receives goods, keeps reserves, schedules deliveries with the carts and horses, and salts meat into barrels.

jobs.name: Herdsman
jobs.description: Tames wild animals, breeds livestock and sends stock to pasture or the butcher.

jobs.name: Shepherd
jobs.description: Keeps the flock: lambing, folding, shearing.

jobs.name: Beekeeper
jobs.description: Keeps skeps for honey and wax.

jobs.name: Tanner
jobs.description: Tans hides into leather, hard leather and parchment; makes leather armour and saddles.

jobs.name: Cook
jobs.description: Cooks pottage and simple bread for the village at the cookhouse.

jobs.name: Husbandman
jobs.description: Plans the rotation and irrigation, keeps seed, directs the farm hands.

jobs.name: Miller
jobs.description: Grinds grain into flour.

jobs.name: Weaver
jobs.description: Spins and weaves flax into linen and wool into woollen cloth; makes tapestry.

jobs.name: Tailor
jobs.description: Sews garb, cloaks, gambesons, banners and flags.

jobs.name: Chandler
jobs.description: Makes candles and torches from wax and tallow.

jobs.name: Herbalist
jobs.description: Tends the wounded and sick with herbs; makes remedies.

jobs.name: Mason
jobs.description: Dresses stone, burns lime, builds hearths, wells, footings and stone upgrades (tiers 3-4).

jobs.name: Potter
jobs.description: Makes pottery, roof tiles and (later) brick.

jobs.name: Bloomer
jobs.description: Smelts ore into iron, gold and silver at the bloomery.

jobs.name: Smith
jobs.description: Forges tools, braziers, spears, axes and maces; makes steel once known.

jobs.name: Watchman
jobs.description: Keeps watch on roads and the village.

jobs.name: Serjeant
jobs.description: Armed and armoured soldier.

jobs.name: Page
jobs.description: Handles the early stages of the colony's accounts.

jobs.name: Squire
jobs.description: Best of the soldiers; the player's personal guard.

jobs.name: Messenger
jobs.description: Carries the lord's letters and accounts to the Count and others. Weeks on the road; can be delayed, waylaid or intercepted.

jobs.name: Clerk
jobs.description: Learns letters and reckoning; copies books.

jobs.name: Schoolmaster
jobs.description: Teaches clerks; raises the village's learning.

jobs.name: Master Carpenter
jobs.description: Fine furniture, wood tools, mill machinery (millwright work).

jobs.name: Bowyer
jobs.description: Makes bows and arrows.

jobs.name: Master Mason
jobs.description: Designs and leads tier 4-5 structures: halls, keeps, walls.

jobs.name: Carver
jobs.description: Fine stonework and furniture; oversees castle block production.

jobs.name: Ingeniator
jobs.description: Works with the master mason on advanced structures; deep mine shoring and drainage, mills, siege works.

jobs.name: Master Cook
jobs.description: Quality meals from higher-tier food.

jobs.name: Baker
jobs.description: Bread and pastry.

jobs.name: Brewster
jobs.description: Ale, mead and cider.

jobs.name: Innkeeper
jobs.description: Runs the inn: food, drink and guest beds. Requires a cook or master cook.

jobs.name: Butcher
jobs.description: Slaughters stock and renders tallow.

jobs.name: Cheesemaker
jobs.description: Cheese from milk and salt.

jobs.name: Draper
jobs.description: Fine clothing; trades cloth.

jobs.name: Leech
jobs.description: Treats the wounded with herbs, bandaging and setting bones.

jobs.name: Chirurgeon
jobs.description: Uses fine tools to treat serious injuries.

jobs.name: Spicer
jobs.description: Makes and sells remedies in quantity.

jobs.name: Armourer
jobs.description: Swords, mail, helms, lances, shields.

jobs.name: Goldsmith
jobs.description: Jewelry and silverware.

jobs.name: Moneyer
jobs.description: Strikes coin from silver and gold.

jobs.name: Chapman
jobs.description: Oversees the movement of goods in his assigned zone, keeps the market, trades with travelling merchants, creates demand for roads.

jobs.name: Forester
jobs.description: Keeper of the forest, its herds and game. Sets protections (no felling fruit trees, no hunting breeding stock), replanting and culling quotas.

jobs.name: Steward
jobs.description: Runs the colony's wider economy: prices, merchant oversight, taxes in kind, provisioning for winter.

jobs.name: Quartermaster
jobs.description: Head of the stockyards and stables late in the game: storage, carts, horses, and provisioning for the army.

jobs.name: Chamberlain
jobs.description: Keeps the coffers, pays wages, collects taxes and tribute.

jobs.name: Bailiff
jobs.description: The lord's officer: low justice among the colonists, the watch, unrest, collecting dues.

jobs.name: Marshal
jobs.description: Commands the army.

jobs.name: Knight
jobs.description: Mounted, armoured warrior; leads men.

jobs.name: Scholar
jobs.description: Advances village knowledge; paid from levies.

jobs.name: Priest
jobs.description: Arrives with the settlers as the lord's advisor. Keeps the chapel, leads worship, comforts the sick and grieving. Secretly the Count's man: he reports on the far lands. He does not research.

resources.name: Water
resources.notes: Drawn on demand from wells and sources.

resources.name: Cart
resources.notes: Two come from the count. Pulled by a horse; the stockman's delivery tool.

resources.name: Cooking Pot
resources.notes: The camp pot; the cook's kit.

resources.name: Tinderbox
resources.notes: Flint and steel for lighting fires.

resources.name: Quern
resources.notes: Hand mill; slow flour before the mills.

fauna.name: Wolf
fauna.behaviour: predator: takes sheep, attacks the lone

deposits.name: Salt Vein
deposits.notes: Until one is mined, salt comes from the count's cart.

recipes.effect: Plants a tree (or fruit tree in an orchard).

recipes.notes: Culling a threat as much as hunting.
Culling a threat as much as hunting.
Culling a threat as much as hunting.

recipes.effect: Deepens the mine one stage / repairs shoring.

recipes.season: sow autumn or spring, reap late summer

recipes.effect: Keeps the horses fit to pull. Unfed horses can't work.
Delivery run: carries several loads at once.
Brings a wild swarm into a skep for the apiary.

recipes.notes: Centralised meat packing: meat and salt into barrels.
Wood stands in for oak bark.
Early, poor tools before the smith.
Hunter makes his own until a bowyer exists.
